title: Steak au Poivre
subtitle: Pepper-crusted sirloin with cream and cognac pan sauce
excerpt: Sirloin steaks pressed into cracked black pepper, seared hard in a very hot pan, then rested while a cream and cognac sauce is made from the pan drippings. One of the great French bistro dishes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Steak au poivre became a Parisian bistro classic in the early 20th century and reached its peak popularity in the 1960s and 1970s. The dish is built around two techniques: the pepper crust, which provides a fiery, aromatic contrast to the beef, and the pan sauce, where cognac, often flambéed, is deglazed with cream and reduced to a glossy, rich sauce. The flambe step is theatrical but optional: the same result is achieved by cooking the cognac without igniting it.

recipeTools.notes: A heavy, wide frying pan, ideally cast iron or stainless, to get a proper crust.

content.text: Use whole black peppercorns and crack them coarsely with a heavy pan or rolling pin. Pre-ground pepper does not work for this dish: you need visible pieces, not dust. Press the pepper firmly into both sides of the steak so it adheres. The pan must be very hot before the steak goes in: a drop of water should evaporate instantly. Sear without moving for 2 to 3 minutes per side for medium-rare in a 3 cm thick steak.

items.preparation: about 250 g each, at room temperature

content.text: Press the cracked pepper firmly onto both sides of each steak. Season with salt. Heat a heavy pan over very high heat until smoking. Add the oil and then the steaks. Sear for 2 to 3 minutes per side for medium-rare, adjusting for thickness. Remove from the pan and rest on a warm plate.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter and shallots to the pan. Cook for 2 minutes. Add the cognac and let it bubble for 1 minute, scraping up any browned bits. Add the cream and simmer for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until the sauce has reduced to a coating consistency. Season with salt.
Place the steaks on warmed plates. Pour the pan sauce over and around. Serve with thin-cut chips or pommes purée.
